summary:
Ankara stands under Turkey's national framework: the sources record no Ankara-level law or municipal measure, and the city's distinct exposure is institutional, since the presidency, the Ministry of Family and the drafting machinery for national legislation sit there. The penal-code package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 is drafted, and would be enforced, through institutions operating in Ankara.

The leaked draft, known as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct treated as contrary to biological sex and general morality, punishable by up to three years in prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, expose health professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison and trans people receiving care the authorities deem illegal to up to three years, and allow courts to order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, which had not been enacted as of the reporting date.

Kaos GL's 2025 annual report concludes that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family, both of them Ankara institutions. It records censored broadcasts, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years, with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report counts six violations of the right to life over the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected group, alongside a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. Turkey compiles no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on the organisation's own monitoring; with no general homicide or violence denominator in the sources, the six deaths cannot be expressed as a rate or compared with the risk borne by the general population.
tangentialFactors:
Both developments in this record are contested or unfinished. The penal-code package remained a draft at its reporting date of 29 October 2025, so its penalties and its age-25 threshold for gender-affirming care cannot be read as the state of the law on a given travel date; the objection filed by fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association shows the provisions were still being fought over.

The monitoring comparison runs in one direction only: torture and ill-treatment violations rose from 51 to 89 year on year, and three of the six right-to-life violations were recorded as hate-motivated. Because the state publishes no hate-crime statistics, the only comparison base available is the monitoring organisation's own previous reports, so trend figures should be read as an NGO series rather than an official record.

For a visitor whose plans involve public events, advocacy organisations or hospital-based care in Ankara, the pressure described here is administrative and political: censorship of broadcasts, bans on artistic events and prosecutions of organisers, all set by offices seated in the city.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ankara live under the same national framework, and the measures in this record reach them through institutions seated in the city. Criminal cases were opened against 11 members of an LGBTI+ association that was closed, the first such closure in years, removing an organising and support channel that people living there had used.

With no official hate-crime statistics compiled, the record of violence against LGBTI+ residents depends on NGO monitoring: six right-to-life violations in the year, three recorded as hate-motivated, trans people the most affected, and torture and ill-treatment violations up from 51 to 89.

If the draft penal-code package is enacted, residents seeking gender-affirming care would face a minimum age of 25, mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, while clinicians treating them risk fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years.

Censored broadcasts and cancelled or banned artistic events narrow the public and cultural space in which LGBTI+ residents can appear openly.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved in the sources. The reporting describes a draft as of 29 October 2025, and no later status appears in the material.

The six right-to-life violations cannot be converted into a rate. The sources give no general homicide or violence denominator for Turkey, and the state compiles no hate-crime statistics, so neither the coverage of the count nor its relation to background violence is established here.

No Ankara ordinance, municipal policy or city-level enforcement instruction appears in the sources; the region's exposure runs through national institutions seated there. The sources do not state how many of the recorded national violations occurred in Ankara, and no figure for the LGBTI+ population of the city is available.

Whether any part of the draft package is already being applied in practice ahead of enactment is not sourced.
